description: We’re a six-person team of third-year students - five from HCMUT and one from the UEH -brought together by a shared curiosity: what if people could hear the planet changing, not just see it?
summary:
First of all, while NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) produces stunning visualizations of Earth's phenomena, a compelling parallel can be drawn to a music video, which stands out through its striking visuals combined with the magnificent sound of a song. Recognizing that there is still a gap in delivering the most immersive user experience, we chose the “Earth Information Jukebox” challenge. We selected three main topics for our project that deeply impact users and translate into a more vibrant audio experience:
A connected atmosphere (DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide)
Change in Night Lights (Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023)
An ocean in motion (Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature)
In the process of transforming this project into a real-world product, we had to put ourselves in the users' shoes to understand their needs and deliver a top-notch, engaging experience. Furthermore, with only two days to complete the project, teamwork skills had to come first. Through this opportunity, in the process of working together, our group also developed a beautiful friendship. Ultimately, our team successfully built an interactive web-based jukebox, a standalone desktop app, a backend API endpoint, and a curated playlist of original, AI-generated audio complete with a detailed breakdown of our creative workflow.
details:
We created "The Earth Information Jukebox" because just like a great music video needs both stunning visuals and a moving song to make you feel something, we wanted to give Earth’s silent data a voice. Our platform pairs NASA’s satellite visualizations with original, AI-generated music, letting people actually hear the rhythm of our changing world across three deeply personal themes: the air we breathe, the city lights that connect us, and the oceans in constant motion.

Science often feels distant, locked behind complex charts and cold numbers. By turning those numbers into music, our project makes climate change something you can feel in your bones, not just read on a screen. Our hope is simple: when people truly feel the pulse of the Earth, they will care enough to protect it.

To transform pixels into sound, our computer vision and image-processing pipelines extract structured numerical features from three NASA datasets:

1. Night Lights (2012–2023 NASA Black Marble): Through grayscale conversion, background subtraction, and intensity normalization, we extract nighttime brightness and spatial changes across regions. In our intended sonification, brighter regions rise into higher musical notes while dimmer areas fall into lower pitches, letting listeners hear over a decade of human expansion

2. Oceans (NASA ECCO2 Sea Surface Temperature): Using color quantization, CIELAB color space transformation, and color matching against NASA's thermal scale (0°C to 32°C), we map warm and cold surface currents. Warmer waters translate into higher notes and smoother transitions, turning global heat redistribution into a flowing melody.

3. Atmospheric CO₂ (NASA GEOS Modeling): Through colorbar calibration, color-to-ppm mapping (380 to 460 ppm), and frame-by-frame analysis, we capture minimum, maximum, and mean concentration shifts. The mean CO₂ level sets the central pitch, the concentration range shapes the melodic spread, and daily atmospheric pulses drive the rhythm.

Across all three datasets, our sound mapping framework translates scientific values into pitch, signal intensity into volume, and temporal fluctuations into rhythm and timbre. Currently, our image-processing pipelines successfully extract these numerical features, while the audio player features an independent demonstration track; our next step is directly linking the extracted data to the audio engine for real-time, data-driven sonification.

Behind the scenes, our team poured two sleepless days into building an interactive web jukebox, a standalone desktop app, and a backend API. We designed the user interface in Figma, built the frontend using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and TypeScript, developed our data-processing pipelines in Python, and leveraged AI audio tools to weave sight and sound together. What makes this project special isn't just the code, but the empathy behind it. We constantly put ourselves in the shoes of everyday listeners, asking what would move them. Somewhere between debugging at 3 AM and celebrating every small breakthrough, we didn't just build a functional product. After all, we built a genuine friendship that gave this project its emotion.
